mappings.note: first a D > 0 check to establish that real roots exist, then COMPLETING THE SQUARE to find them; the frame has no outcome for completing the square, so LO-4 carries it as the formula's own method (gap reported)
areas and perimeters of two squares translated into y^2 + 6y - 216 = 0, factorised, and the negative side length rejected; the admissibility judgement is what makes it C-2.2-LO-6
two digit-conditions turned into place-value equations, one of which is quadratic in y; the digit y = 0 is rejected as inadmissible, then factorisation finishes it
reciprocal difference modelled as x^2 + 5x - 50 = 0; the word NATURAL in the stem is what rules out x = -10, an explicit admissibility test
three consecutive integers parametrised as x, x+1, x+2; the fractional root -11/2 is rejected because the stem demands positive integers
the simplest translation in the block, x(x+1) = 306, with the negative root discarded; still a modelling item rather than a bare factorisation exercise
the digit product is substituted into the reversal condition to produce x^2 + 5x - 14 = 0; the negative root cannot be a digit, so admissibility again decides
sum of squares of consecutive naturals gives x^2 + x - 210 = 0; distinguished from the product-of-consecutives item only by the condition, but the same two outcomes
a fraction-plus-reciprocal condition gives 11x^2 - 26x - 21 = 0, which the key resolves by the formula rather than by splitting; the non-integer root is rejected as a numerator
the graded work is translating two fractions and their sum into a quadratic; the key is cut off before naming a solving method, so no solving outcome is claimed
duplicate stem of the natural-numbers reciprocal item but worded as 'two numbers', which weakens the ground for rejecting -10; same translation and factorisation outcomes
asks ONLY to represent the situation as a quadratic equation and stops there -- the pure translate half of LO-6, with no root found and no admissibility to judge
a speed-time-distance model where the 48-minute saving must be converted to 4/5 hour before the quadratic appears; the negative speed is then rejected
price-and-quantity model: 600/(x-5) - 600/x = 4 cleared to x^2 - 5x - 750 = 0; a negative price is inadmissible, so only one root survives
budget-per-day model giving x^2 + 3x - 180 = 0; the same reciprocal-difference structure as the speed items but applied to expenses
sum and product of two ages give x^2 - 35x + 150 = 0, and BOTH roots are positive -- the rejection here is contextual (a father cannot be 5), which is exactly LO-6's admissibility clause
the classic camel problem needs a square-root substitution y = sqrt(x) before it is quadratic at all; the negative y is rejected because a square root cannot be negative
marks in two subjects with a shifted product; unusually BOTH roots are admissible and the answer reports two valid mark pairs, which is a genuine variation on the admissibility theme
cost-per-book model giving x^2 + 10x - 600 = 0; a count of books cannot be negative, so -30 is discarded

two trains with a speed difference and a time difference; the key silently works a 600 km journey against the 60 km printed in the stem (defect reported), but the modelling and factorisation outcomes are unaffected
the model x = 2592/(x/2) reduces to x^2 = 5184 and is finished by a square root -- no factorisation, no formula and no discriminant, so only the translation outcome genuinely applies
upstream/downstream model that collapses to x^2 = 25; the negative stream speed is rejected, but as with the odometer-style items no solving technique beyond a square root is exercised
two taps modelled by rates per hour giving 4t^2 - 23t + 15 = 0; the root t = 3/4 is rejected because it would make the faster tap's time negative -- a contextual, not a sign, rejection
the same two-tap rate model with a plus-3 offset, giving 13x^2 - 41x - 120 = 0; the negative root is inadmissible as a time
work-rate model giving x^2 - 14x + 24 = 0 with both roots positive; x = 2 is rejected because it would make Ram's time negative, another purely contextual admissibility decision
